hookLine: A twenty-one dollar bag, a two dollar test, and a pink liquid that turned blue in a Houston parking lot: Amy Albritton pleaded guilty to a crime the laboratory would later prove had never happened.

captions.text: In August 2010, in a strip-mall parking lot in Houston, Amy Albritton watched a
police officer drop a crumb from her car floor into a vial of pink liquid.
If it stayed pink, she could go home.
It turned blue.
He held the vial up in front of her face and said two words: you're busted.
She was not driving.
Nine hours later she was booked into the Harris County jail, and inside two days she
had pleaded guilty to felony cocaine possession.
But the crumb was not cocaine.
It wasn't a drug at all — and the state's own laboratory would prove it, six months
after she had already confessed to it in open court.
In one American county, two hundred and twelve people were convicted the same way
she was, on evidence a laboratory later found was not a controlled substance at all
— and the two-dollar kit that did it is still in patrol cars across the country
tonight.
Houston, Texas.
Late afternoon, August 2010.
Amy Albritton managed an apartment complex in Monroe, Louisiana.
It was called Frances Place — a well-kept brick building — and she had run it for
two years.
The job came with an apartment.
Hold on to that, because it means she did not have a job and a home as two separate
things.
She had one thing, and it was both.
She had two sons; the younger had been disabled from birth.
Her mother, a pharmacy technician, had died of colon cancer.
Her father had raised her on a single piece of advice about American law, and we
will come back to it.
She was in Houston that August with a man she had been seeing for about a month.
He was driving her white Chrysler Concorde; she was in the passenger seat.
Late in the afternoon he changed lanes, and to this day she cannot say whether he
signalled.
The lights came on behind them, and he pulled into a strip-mall parking lot.
The officer's report records that when he reached the car he saw a needle in the
ceiling lining.
He asked the driver to step out.
The driver got out.
The officer leaned in over the driver's seat, looked around, and called to his
partner.
What the search turned up was this.
A needle.
A packet of BC Powder, an over-the-counter headache remedy sold in every drugstore
in the American South.
And, on the floor, a small white crumb.
None of that is a crime.
A crumb is not a crime, a headache powder is not a crime, and a needle on its own is
not a felony.
To make any of it into a charge, somebody has to say what the crumb is.
In 2010, in one of the largest police departments in America, saying what a crumb
was took about ninety seconds and cost two dollars.
The officer went to the trunk of the patrol car and came back with a small plastic
pouch.
Inside the pouch was a glass vial of pink liquid.
He opened the lid and dropped a piece of the crumb in.
That is the entire procedure.
No machine, no reading, no printout, no second opinion.
There is a colour.
If it stayed pink, everyone could go home.
If it turned blue, then Amy Albritton — the owner of the car, sitting in the
passenger seat of her own vehicle — became a felony defendant.
It turned blue.
He waved the vial in front of her face.
Then, on the evidence submission form, in his own handwriting, he wrote down the
weight of what he had found: point-oh-two grams of crack cocaine.
It was a figure written in ink at the side of a road, and it became the first
official number in the file.
Keep two numbers running through this film, because the whole story sits in the gap
between them.
The first is the one the officer wrote down that afternoon.
The second is the one a chemist would write down six months later.
She was handcuffed in the parking lot.
Both of them were taken in.
And at the jail, before anything else happened, she was strip-searched.
Years later, asked about it, she answered in seven words.
Oh, yes — with the bend over, cough.
She was booked into the Harris County jail at three thirty-seven in the morning,
nine hours after the stop.
In a property room, in a sealed envelope, sat a crumb nobody had examined with
anything more sophisticated than a colour.
In the morning she met her lawyer for the first time.
His name was Dan Richardson, the court had appointed him, and he had a lot of
clients that day.
Everybody in that building does.
He told her what she was charged with: possession of a controlled substance, crack
cocaine.
A felony.
The maximum penalty was two years in a Texas state prison.
By her account he did not ask her what had actually happened, and he did not ask
whether she believed she was innocent.
What he told her was that the prosecutor had already made an offer, and it was for a
great deal less than two years.
Plead guilty, and the sentence would be forty-five days in the county jail — of
which she would probably serve about half.
Now do the arithmetic she had to do, standing in a corridor in the clothes she was
arrested in.
Fighting it meant staying in custody, because she could not post the bond.
It meant a trial in a county she did not live in, hundreds of miles from her sons,
against a police officer with a positive drug test and a signed report.
It meant losing the job for certain — and the job was the apartment.
And if she lost, it meant two years.
Or she could say a sentence that was not true and be out in three weeks.
There is a phrase for what happened next that makes it sound like a decision.
It was not a decision.
It was arithmetic, and the arithmetic only has one answer.
A guilty plea in an American courtroom is not a shrug.
It is a formal act.
The defendant makes a series of statements that function as a confession, and gives
up a list of constitutional rights one at a time, out loud.
Judge Vanessa Velasquez took her through the recitation.
The record notes something the judge never asked about: why the woman in front of
her could not stop crying long enough to finish a sentence.
She was sentenced to forty-five days.
She served twenty-one.
And here is the finding that turns one woman's terrible week into a machine.
When investigators later went back through these cases — the ones where the
laboratory eventually said there had been no drug at all — they measured how long it
had taken those innocent people to plead guilty.
The median was four days.
Fifty-eight per cent of them pleaded guilty at the first opportunity they had, at
arraignment, the very first time they stood in front of a judge.
Then they measured the people who really had been carrying drugs.
That median was twenty-two days.
The innocent plead five times faster than the guilty.
That is not a paradox; it is the system working as designed.
If you are guilty you have reason to wait — evidence to suppress, a witness to
challenge, time to bargain.
If you are innocent and poor, waiting costs everything and buys nothing, because a
positive test is already in the file and there is no laboratory report in there to
argue with.
This was not a Houston peculiarity.
In 2011 a national study commissioned by the Justice Department found that
prosecutors in nine out of ten jurisdictions surveyed accepted guilty pleas on
nothing but the result of a field test.
Not the laboratory.
The colour.
There is one more thing in her file, and it belongs here rather than anywhere else.
Two years before Houston, in Louisiana, she had pleaded guilty to a misdemeanour
drunk-driving charge.
Her breathalyzer reading was zero point zero.
She pleaded guilty to that too.
Same arithmetic, smaller scale, smaller machine.
And it is why, when her father's line comes back, it lands the way it does.
If the law said you had crack, he had told her, you had crack.
She got out after twenty-one days with nowhere to go.
She was fired.
Her furniture and everything else she owned were carried out and put on the side of
the road.
So what is the thing in the plastic pouch.
It is a glass ampoule of a chemical called cobalt thiocyanate, and it is pink.
Chemists have known for well over forty years that when cocaine meets it, a blue
colour forms.
That is the whole science.
Drop the sample in, break the ampoule, watch the colour.
It is that simple because it was designed to be simple.
In 1973 — the same year Richard Nixon formally created the Drug Enforcement
Administration and declared, in his words, an all-out global war on the drug menace
— two California inventors patented what they called a disposable comparison
detector kit.
A pouch.
A vial.
Open it, add the substance, seal it, break the glass, watch the colours change.
An officer could carry a dozen in a glove box.
It spread across the country almost immediately, carrying something more useful than
accuracy: the appearance of science.
A chemical, a reaction, a result.
A laboratory in the palm of a hand.
Within a year, the people whose actual job was measurement said so out loud.
In 1974 the National Bureau of Standards studied the kits and wrote that they should
not be used as sole evidence for the identification of a narcotic or drug of abuse.
Four years later the Department of Justice reached its own conclusion: field tests
should not be used for evidential purposes.
Nineteen seventy-eight.
That is the year the American government determined, in writing, that this test does
not prove anything.
Amy Albritton was arrested on one thirty-two years later.
The problem is not that the test is fake.
The problem is that the colour is not exclusive.
Cobalt thiocyanate turns blue for cocaine — and it also turns blue for more than
eighty other compounds, among them methadone, certain acne medications, and several
common household cleaners.
One manufacturer keeps a list of more than fifty perfectly legal substances that
will set off its own products.
In one manufacturer's own kits, chocolate produces a colour close to the one heroin
produces.
Which is why the results are inadmissible at trial in nearly every jurisdiction in
the United States.
A prosecutor cannot stand in front of a jury and offer a colour as proof.
Read those two sentences together and you have the whole film.
The evidence is not good enough for a trial.
It is good enough for a conviction.
Because drug possession cases do not go to trial.
Police arrest more than one point two million people a year for illegal drug
possession; drug charges account for more than one in ten of all county and state
felony convictions; and at least ninety per cent of those convictions arrive by plea
deal.
In Harris County, Texas, in this period, the figure was ninety-nine and a half per
cent.
The courtroom where a field test would be thrown out is a room almost nobody ever
reaches.
The man who invented the test Houston was using has a name.
L. J. Scott, Junior, developed it in 1973 while he was working for the DEA, and in
1990 he founded his own company.
The Houston Police Department became his longest-standing major customer.
In 2014, the last year for which records were available, Houston bought nine
thousand of his kits.
And here is the part that is hard to shake.
Scott knew a single reaction was not enough, so he had built a better version.
Three steps.
Cobalt thiocyanate first, for the blue.
Then hydrochloric acid, which turns the solution pink again and eliminates a whole
class of impostors.
Then chloroform, which splits a genuine positive into two clean layers — blue below,
pink above.
Much harder to fool.
When he started his own business, he went back to the single chemical interaction.
The one-step test.
The record does not say why, and neither will we.
Asked about all of this, the man who made them said it plainly: no field test is
fail safe; any field test can give you an erroneous result.
Asked whether a laboratory ought to confirm every field test before anyone is
convicted on it, he answered in six words.
I would.
But that's just me.
His company's own website put the risk inside a parenthesis: it is possible, though
unlikely, to receive a false positive result under certain conditions.
And when reporters checked the labels, the three largest manufacturers carried no
false-positive warning at all — one of them added one only after it was asked.
Everyone in this chain — the inventor, the manufacturers, the Bureau of Standards,
the Justice Department — had been saying the same thing for four decades.
Confirm it in a laboratory.
In Amy Albritton's case, somebody eventually did.
On the twenty-third of February 2011, an analyst named Ahtavea Barker sat down at
the Houston Police Department crime laboratory with the evidence from a traffic stop
the previous August, and did what a field kit cannot do.
She ran it through a gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer, an instrument that
separates a sample into its components and identifies each one by its molecular
fingerprint.
It does not report a colour.
It reports what a thing is.
The white powder came back first: aspirin and caffeine.
The ingredients of BC Powder.
Exactly what the packet said it was.
The needle had too little residue on it even to test.
In the words of the investigation that later found this file: it was just a syringe.
Then the crumb.
The fragmentation pattern did not match cocaine.
It did not match any other compound in the laboratory's database — and that database
is enormous.
It was not a drug.
It did not contain anything mixed with a drug.
It was, the reporters who read the file wrote, a crumb.
Food debris, perhaps.
On the examination sheet, Barker wrote the finding in the laboratory's shorthand.
N.A.M. — no acceptable match.
And then: N.C.S. No controlled substance identified.
And she wrote the weight.
The officer at the roadside had put down point-oh-two grams.
The scale in the laboratory measured what was left at zero point zero one three four
grams.
About the same, Barker noted, as a tiny pinch of salt.
That is the object at the centre of this story.
A pinch of salt's worth of something that was not a drug, on the floor of a car she
was not driving, in a state she did not live in.
By the time that report existed, Amy Albritton had been out of jail for five months.
She had lost her job, her apartment and her furniture, and she was a convicted felon
in the state of Texas.
Then nothing happened, because of a detail so mundane it is almost the whole
scandal: laboratories rarely notify officers when a false positive comes back.
The report was filed.
It was correct.
It was six months late, and it was addressed to nobody.
She spent the next years learning what a felony record does to an ordinary working
life.
A convenience store with hours that changed every week.
Bartending.
Waiting tables.
Eventually managing property again, in Baton Rouge, for a landlord whose buildings
nobody else wanted, at a wage that did not include an apartment.
Tips included, she was earning about fifteen thousand dollars a year.
She liked her co-workers.
She impressed her bosses.
She could not rent in her own name, because no landlord takes a drug felon.
Now the story stops being about one woman.
In Harris County, the District Attorney's office had begun to notice something in
its own paperwork.
A case would close with a guilty plea, and then, weeks or months later, a laboratory
report would arrive saying the evidence was not what the defendant had confessed to
possessing.
The office had a name for the mismatch.
It called them variants.
District Attorney Devon Anderson hired a former prosecutor, Marie Munier, to go back
through the files and count them.
The conviction integrity unit, run by a prosecutor named Inger Chandler, took what
she found.
Between January 2004 and June 2015, the office had failed to correct four hundred
and sixteen variants.
Every single one had ended in a guilty plea.
Some were ambiguous — positive for the wrong drug, or the wrong weight, or too
little left to analyse at all.
But in two hundred and fifty-one of them the result was not ambiguous in the
slightest.
The laboratory's finding, in the office's own file, was the same three words that
were on Amy Albritton's sheet.
No controlled substance.
Three hundred and one of the four hundred and sixteen had begun as arrests by the
Houston Police Department.
Of those three hundred and one, two hundred and twelve were built on evidence the
laboratory determined was not a controlled substance.
All two hundred and twelve of those people pleaded guilty.
Ninety-three per cent were sentenced to jail or prison.
Fifty of them had no prior drug conviction of any kind.
Two more numbers belong here, without commentary.
Fifty-nine per cent of the wrongfully convicted were Black, in a city whose Black
population is twenty-four per cent.
And sixty-three per cent of the cases involved less than a single gram of evidence.
Less than a gram.
That is the entire category.
Not kilos in a trunk — crumbs, residue, powder in a fold of paper.
And notice who found this.
Not a defence campaign, not a newspaper, not a federal investigation.
The office that won every one of those convictions went back through its own files
and counted its own errors.
The institution that convicted them is the institution that found them.
What it did next was slower.
By the summer of 2016, the integrity unit had struck one hundred and nineteen
no-controlled-substance convictions from the record.
At least a hundred and seventy-two more were still standing.
One of the letters had gone out on the twenty-ninth of July 2014.
It was a form letter — Munier was sending hundreds of them — and it opened with the
salutation "Dear Sir or Madam.
The body of it was not generic at all.
It told the recipient that the Harris County District Attorney's office had learned
the drug evidence in her case was not a controlled substance.
And then this sentence: accordingly, you were prosecuted for a criminal drug offense
and convicted in error.
It was posted to the address on her driver's licence.
She was not there.
That address was the apartment that came with the job, and the job had ended the day
she pleaded guilty.
The letter telling Amy Albritton she had been convicted in error was mailed to the
home the conviction took away from her.
She found out from reporters, years late.
Her answer was six words.
I knew it!
I told them!
Her conviction was eventually set aside.
In March 2016 a reporter sat down with the man who had run the Houston Police
Department through all of this.
Charles McClelland had been its chief of police, and he was asked about the
two-dollar kits his officers carried.
He did not defend them.
What he said was this.
Police officers aren't chemists.
We shouldn't be doing field tests on the hood of patrol cars.
That is a chief of police, on the record, saying the procedure that convicted two
hundred and twelve people in his own city should never have been performed by his
own officers.
He went further: if he had known about the false positives his department was
generating, he said, he would have ordered a halt to all field testing across the
entire force.
If he had known.
Nine thousand of those kits a year went out of that department's supply room.
One was opened at the side of a road in August 2010 and held up in front of a woman
sitting in her own car.
The laboratory results had been coming back for over a decade.
Nobody told the chief, because the system contained no step in which anybody had to.
So what changed.
In 2015, District Attorney Devon Anderson issued the reform that should have existed
for forty years: her office would no longer take a guilty plea in a drug possession
case before the laboratory had issued its report.
She described what had happened in her county as a breakdown at every point in the
system.
Read the timing of that rule and the trap is visible.
Laboratories typically issue a report in about two weeks.
Defendants usually see a judge within three days.
For decades the plea had simply been faster than the truth.
Anderson's rule made the truth go first.
In December 2016 a Texas state panel — the Timothy Cole Exoneration Review
Commission, eleven members including legislators, a criminal appellate judge,
prosecutors, police officers and forensic scientists — recommended that the state
require laboratory testing in every case built on a drug field test.
Its own words: requiring laboratory testing of all drug field tests will reduce the
risk of wrongfully arresting and convicting an individual of being in possession of
a controlled substance.
The following year the Texas legislature passed House Bill 34, titled "An act
relating to measures to prevent wrongful convictions," effective September 2017.
Section 8 of that act directed the Texas Forensic Science Commission to study drug
field test kits — their quality, accuracy and reliability, and the common problems
with them — and report back by December 2018.
A study.
Not a requirement.
The state that produced hundreds of these convictions answered its own commission by
commissioning more reading.
In July 2017 the Houston Police Department itself did stop, ending its longstanding
practice of using the two-dollar kits to make drug arrests.
Chief Art Acevedo said officers would rely instead on their own expertise — they
have, he said, a wealth of training and experience into what narcotics look like,
what they feel like in terms of the packaging, the colour, the appearance.
And the stated reason was not accuracy.
It was officer safety: the fear that handling street fentanyl to run a colour test
would poison the officer running it.
The kits stopped in Houston because they had become dangerous to police.
Not because they had become dangerous to everybody else.
Elsewhere the count kept climbing.
By 2020 more than two hundred and fifty wrongful convictions had been overturned in
Houston alone, and prosecutors in Las Vegas and in Multnomah County, Oregon, had
begun vacating their own.
Judges began to move, slowly.
In 2018, in Imperial County, California, Judge Christopher Plourd ruled that one
widely used brand of field test does not meet a scientific admissibility standard.
In 2021 a Massachusetts judge named Brian David ordered the state's Department of
Correction to stop using its kits on prisoners' mail, calling the practice arbitrary
and unlawful guesswork — and he had a measurement to work from.
Over a single year, laboratory analysis of that mail found thirty-eight per cent of
the items testing positive contained no drug at all.
One manufacturer's own answer is the one that has always been available to all of
them, and it is technically correct: field tests are specifically not intended to be
used as a factor in the decision to prosecute or convict a suspect.
Which raises the only question that matters.
If nobody intends them to convict anyone, why do they.
Here is the answer.
The kits were never withdrawn.
No federal agency regulates their use.
There is no national training standard for the officers who carry them, and many get
little or none.
And nothing in American law required a laboratory to confirm a field test before a
person pleaded guilty on it.
Meanwhile the machine kept running.
In January 2024 the Quattrone Center for the Fair Administration of Justice at the
University of Pennsylvania measured it.
Of the more than one and a half million drug arrests made in America every year,
roughly seven hundred and seventy-three thousand involve a colour-based field test.
Roughly thirty thousand people a year are falsely implicated by one.
Ninety per cent of prosecutors still accept a guilty plea without laboratory
confirmation.
Forty-six per cent of laboratories do not run the confirmation at all once a plea
has been filed — the case is closed, and the truth is no longer needed.
And Black Americans are arrested on a false positive at roughly three times the rate
of white Americans.
The study's lead author put the design fault in one sentence: presumptive field drug
test kits are known to produce false-positive errors and were never designed or
intended to provide conclusive evidence of drug presence.
Thirty thousand people a year.
That is not a backlog of old cases.
That is this year, and next year.
Then, this spring, one state did something.
On the twenty-sixth of March 2026 the Governor of Colorado signed House Bill
26-1020, passed sixty-five to nothing in the House and thirty-three to nothing in
the Senate.
Police there may no longer arrest a person for misdemeanour drug possession where a
colour-change field test is the only basis — they must issue a summons instead.
Before a defendant pleads, the court must tell them the test has a known error rate.
And the right to demand a laboratory is written into the statute.
Colorado is the first state to put any of that into law.
Fifty-three years after the patent, forty-eight years after the Justice Department
said these tests should not be used for evidential purposes, and ten years after an
investigation counted the convictions in one Texas county.
One state, out of fifty.
So what did the set-aside fix.
Asked that, she said: no — you're not ever free and clear of it, it follows you
everywhere you go.
A vacated conviction does not give back a job, or an apartment that came with the
job, or the furniture carried out to the kerb, or the years at fifteen thousand
dollars, or the applications declined by landlords who ran a background check and
did not read to the end.
It does not un-say the statements she made in that courtroom while a judge waited
for her to stop crying.
And it does not undo what she had been taught before any of it began.
If the law said you had crack, her father had told her, you had crack.
Go back to the object one last time.
A crumb, on the floor of a car, at the side of a road in Houston.
An officer looked at it and wrote point-oh-two grams.
A chemist put it on a scale six months later and wrote zero point zero one three
four grams — a pinch of salt — and beside it, three words: no controlled substance.
Between those two numbers sat forty-five days, twenty-one days served, a job, a
home, and a felony record for life.
Nobody was disciplined.
Nobody lost a job over it except her.
No court ever found that the officer did anything wrong.
That is the point, and it is harder than a villain would be: nothing here required
anyone to break a rule.
Every person in the chain did what the system permitted, and the system permitted
this.
Somewhere tonight an officer will open a small plastic pouch at the side of a road,
drop something in, and watch the colour.
It costs two dollars.
It is the same chemistry it was in 1973.
And whoever is in that passenger seat will find out, the way Amy Albritton did, that
in the space between a colour and a laboratory there is room for a whole life to
fall through.
If you think nobody should be a felon before the evidence has been tested, hit like
— and stay for the next one, because the machine in this story is still running.
